113.title: A blessing for each food
113.hook: bread, grain, wine, tree fruit, earth fruit and everything else each have their own blessing
113.howItsDone: Before eating, observant Jews say the blessing that matches the food, bread, other grain foods, wine, tree fruit, earth fruit, or everything else, and the bread blessing covers the rest of a meal with bread.

segments.voice: Yesterday, baruch, the six words that open almost every blessing. Your line was six words before anything. Now, what comes after the six? Day one hundred thirteen.

Put a Jewish grandmother at a kitchen table with an apple, a strawberry, a slice of bread, a cookie, a glass of wine and a piece of cheese, and ask her to bless them. She won't say the same thing six times. She'll say six different endings. The apple gets one. The strawberry gets another, and it's not the same as the apple. The cookie and the bread aren't the same either, though they're both made from flour. It sounds like a quiz. It's really a way of looking at what's on your plate. Today: hamotzi, and its cousins.
screen: `SIX FOODS ON A KITCHEN TABLE.` → `SIX DIFFERENT ENDINGS.` → `A WAY OF LOOKING AT YOUR PLATE.`

segments.voice: After the six opening words, each food gets its own ending. Bread: hamotzi lechem min ha'aretz, who brings forth bread from the earth. The words come from a psalm that says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, God makes things grow "to bring forth bread out of the earth." Other grain foods, like cake, cookies or pasta: borei minei mezonot, who creates kinds of nourishment. Wine and grape juice: borei pri hagafen, who creates the fruit of the vine. Fruit from a tree: borei pri ha'etz. Fruit and vegetables from the ground: borei pri ha'adamah, the fruit of the earth. And everything else, cheese, eggs, water, candy: shehakol nihyeh bidvaro, by whose word all things came to be. So the apple gets tree, and the strawberry gets earth, because it grows on a low plant. A banana, surprisingly, gets earth too, since the plant it grows on isn't a tree in the rabbis' sense: it doesn't keep its trunk year to year. The Talmud asks why bless food at all, and it notices two verses that seem to disagree. One psalm says: "The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof." Another says: "the earth hath He given to the children of men." Which is it? The Talmud's answer: before the blessing, it's God's. After the blessing, it's been given to you. Eating without a blessing, the Talmud says, is like taking from something holy without asking. The blessing is how you ask. And the endings make you look closely: where did this grow, on a tree, in the ground, from grain? Every meal becomes a little map of the world.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: match a blessing to one food today. Let's warm up now. Settle, and breathe. Picture the next thing you'll eat. Now trace it back. Did it grow on a tree, like an apple or an orange? In the ground, like a potato, a tomato, a strawberry? From grain, like bread or pasta? Or is it something else, like cheese or an egg? Name its category, tree, earth, grain, bread, vine or everything else. If you pray, you can say its blessing when you eat it. If not, just pause and name where it came from. The bell holds the time.
Hamotzi. Who brings forth bread from the earth: the blessing over bread, one of six endings, each food with its own word.
Your line: each food has its word. Today, before you eat, name where the food grew, even silently. Day one hundred thirteen.

114.title: A hundred blessings a day (Menachot 43b)
114.hook: the Talmud teaches a person should say a hundred blessings each day
114.howItsDone: Jews who pray the three daily services, with the morning blessings and blessings over food, reach about a hundred blessings a day; on Shabbat some add blessings over fruit or spices to complete the count.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hamotzi and its cousins: tree, earth, vine, grain, bread and everything else. Your line was each food has its word. Did you name one? Day one hundred fourteen.

People count all kinds of things now. Steps. Calories. Hours of sleep. Minutes of screen time, usually with a little shame attached. Ten thousand steps a day has become a kind of modern commandment, even though the number came from a marketing campaign. Long before step counters, the rabbis of the Talmud set a daily goal too. Not steps. Blessings. A hundred of them, every day. Today: a hundred blessings a day.
screen: `STEPS, CALORIES, SCREEN TIME.` → `TEN THOUSAND STEPS.` → `A HUNDRED BLESSINGS.`

segments.voice: The source is a single line in the Talmud, in a discussion about something else entirely. Rabbi Meir says a person is obligated to say a hundred blessings every day. And his proof is a piece of wordplay. In Deuteronomy, Moses asks the people, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And now, Israel, what doth the LORD thy God require of thee." In Hebrew, what is mah. Rabbi Meir reads it as if it were me'ah, a hundred. What does God ask of you? A hundred. Later tradition added a story: that in King David's time, a hundred people were dying every day from a plague, and David set a hundred blessings a day, and the dying stopped. It's told as tradition; the Bible itself doesn't say it. How do you get to a hundred? It's not as hard as it sounds, if you pray the daily services. The morning blessings alone are over a dozen: for waking, for eyes that see, for clothes, for the ground under your feet. The central standing prayer has nineteen blessings, said three times a day. Add the blessings before and after food, Asher Yatzar, and the others, and a person who prays the full day reaches about a hundred. On Shabbat, the standing prayer is shorter, so some people eat an extra piece of fruit or smell spices to make up the count. It's a lovely picture: counting thanks the way we count steps. And even if you never say a formal blessing, the idea travels. A hundred times a day, notice something you didn't make, and say so.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count the thanks you give today. Start the count now. Settle, and breathe. Thank you for this breath. That's one. For the chair holding you up. Two. For your eyes, or your ears, whichever is bringing you this. Three. Keep going quietly, at your own pace: water, a person, a memory, light, a roof. Count them on your fingers if you like. You won't reach a hundred in two minutes. See how far you get. The bell holds the time.
A hundred blessings a day. Rabbi Meir's daily count, read out of one Hebrew word: what, mah, heard as a hundred, me'ah.
screen: `A HUNDRED BLESSINGS A DAY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a hundred small thanks. Today, keep the count going. Tally them in your notes app or on your fingers, and see where you are by bedtime. Day one hundred fourteen.

115.title: Blessing after eating (Deuteronomy 8:10)
115.hook: the one blessing the Torah itself commands: eat, be satisfied, and bless
115.howItsDone: After a meal with bread, observant Jews say Birkat Hamazon, often led by one person when three or more have eaten together; after other foods they say a shorter blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hundred blessings a day, from one word read two ways. Your line was a hundred small thanks. How far did your count get? Day one hundred fifteen.

Think about the moment right after a big meal. Thanksgiving, a wedding, a birthday dinner. Your belt feels tight. Someone's already clearing plates. Everybody's drifting toward the couch or the car. When you were hungry, you'd have thanked anyone for a piece of bread. Now that you're full, the thanks is the last thing on your mind. Here's a surprise about Jewish blessings over food: the blessings before eating were set by the rabbis. The one blessing the Torah itself commands comes after. Today: Birkat Hamazon, the blessing after eating.
screen: `RIGHT AFTER A BIG MEAL.` → `THANKS IS THE LAST THING ON YOUR MIND.` → `THE TORAH COMMANDS THE AFTER.`

segments.voice: The verse is in Deuteronomy, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God for the good land which He hath given thee." Eat. Be satisfied. Then bless. And a few verses later, the Torah explains why the order matters. It warns: when you've eaten and are satisfied, and built good houses, and your flocks and silver and gold have grown, be careful that your heart doesn't grow proud and forget. Hunger reminds you to be grateful. Fullness makes you forget. So the Torah puts the blessing right at the moment you're most likely to skip it. Birkat hamazon means the blessing for food. It's a longer grace, with four main blessings, and the Talmud gives each one a history. The first, for God who feeds the whole world, it credits to Moses, when the manna fell. The second, for the land, to Joshua, when the people entered it. The third, for Jerusalem, to David and Solomon. And the fourth, for God who is good and does good, the rabbis added after a terrible defeat, when the bodies of the fallen were finally allowed burial, a thanks said even out of grief. So one after-dinner grace carries the whole story from the desert to the rabbis. When three or more eat together, one person invites the others to bless, and they answer, like a small congregation around a table. On Shabbat and holidays many begin by singing a psalm about coming home from exile. After smaller snacks there are shorter blessings. But the idea is the same: when you're full, that's the moment to say thank you.
screen: `EAT, BE SATISFIED, AND BLESS.` · `FULLNESS MAKES YOU FORGET.` · `FOUR BLESSINGS, FOUR HISTORIES.` · `THREE AT A TABLE: LET US BLESS.` · then, large: `FULL, THEN GRATEFUL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give thanks after a meal, not just before. Think back to the last thing you ate. Settle, and breathe. Where did it come from? Who grew it, carried it, cooked it? How did it feel to be full, or at least not hungry? If you pray, you can offer thanks to God for it now, in your own words, or with the old verse: eat, be satisfied, and bless. If you don't, simply thank whoever made the meal possible, in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Birkat Hamazon. The blessing after eating: the one food blessing the Torah itself commands, said when you're full.
Your line: full, then grateful. Today, after one meal, before you get up from the table, say thank you out loud, to God, to the cook, or to both. Day one hundred fifteen.

116.title: For firsts
116.hook: a blessing for new things, new seasons and first times each year
116.carry: you kept me alive for this
116.howItsDone: Jews say Shehecheyanu on the first night of festivals, at the first Hanukkah candle, over a fruit's first eating in its season, over significant new clothes or a new home, and at many of life's firsts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Birkat Hamazon, the blessing after eating. Your line was full, then grateful. Did you say thank you before leaving the table? Day one hundred sixteen.

The first strawberries of the summer. The first snow. The first time you hold a baby niece. The first night in a new apartment, eating takeout on the floor because the table hasn't arrived. Firsts have their own feeling: a little shock of joy, and underneath it, a quiet thought. I made it to this. Plenty of people didn't. Plenty of years I wasn't sure I would. Jewish tradition has a blessing for exactly that feeling, and it's one of the most loved in the whole tradition. Today: Shehecheyanu.
screen: `THE FIRST STRAWBERRIES.` → `THE FIRST NIGHT IN A NEW PLACE.` → `I MADE IT TO THIS.`

segments.voice: After the six opening words, the blessing says: shehecheyanu, v'kiyemanu, v'higianu lazman hazeh. Who has kept us alive, and sustained us, and brought us to this time. Three verbs. Kept us alive: you're still here. Sustained us, or held us up: through everything in between. Brought us to this season: to this exact moment. When is it said? The Talmud and later law list many moments. On the first night of each festival, over the candles or the wine. At the first lighting of the Hanukkah candles. When you eat a fruit for the first time in its season, the first cherries, the first pomegranate of the year. When you put on important new clothes, or buy a new home, or major new things you're glad of. When you see a close friend you haven't seen in a month. And people say it at life's firsts, when a baby is born, at a graduation, a wedding, or the first time they do something they never thought they'd get to. Notice what the blessing is not about. It isn't about the strawberry being good, or the dress being nice. It's about time. It says: there was a season when this was out of reach, and I've been carried here. The Talmud even says a person can say it over a new fruit the moment they see it in the market, before buying it, because the joy is in the arrival. Some people keep a fruit they haven't tasted all year for the second night of Rosh Hashanah, just so they have a reason to say it. A blessing so good that people go looking for excuses.
screen: `KEPT ALIVE, SUSTAINED, BROUGHT HERE.` · `FESTIVALS, FRUIT, NEW CLOTHES.` · `LIFE'S FIRSTS.` · `A BLESSING ABOUT TIME.` · then, large: `BROUGHT US TO THIS SEASON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say it for one first today. Let's find the first. Settle, and breathe. Think back over this season. What's new? The first cold morning, a first conversation with someone, a first bite of something, a first day without pain, a first attempt at something. Pick one. Then think back to when it was out of reach. If you pray, you can say the blessing, or just its English: who kept us alive and brought us to this time. If you don't, say it plainly: I made it to this. The bell holds the time.
Shehecheyanu. Who has kept us alive, sustained us, and brought us to this time: the blessing for firsts and new seasons.
Your line: you kept me alive for this. Today, when anything is new, say the line, even silently. Day one hundred sixteen.

117.title: Blessings for wonders
117.hook: there are blessings for lightning, thunder, the sea, a rainbow and trees in blossom
117.carry: the world has blessings built in
117.howItsDone: Jews say short blessings on seeing lightning, hearing thunder, seeing the sea or a rainbow, and once a year on seeing fruit trees in blossom in the spring month of Nisan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shehecheyanu, the blessing for firsts. Your line was you kept me alive for this. What was your first? Day one hundred seventeen.

You're driving home in a summer storm. The sky goes white for half a second, and you count, the way you did as a kid: one Mississippi, two Mississippi, and then the thunder rolls over the car. Or you're on a beach at the end of a long drive, and there it is, the whole sea at once. Or a rainbow, and everyone in the parking lot pulls out their phones. There are moments when the world stops you in your tracks. Jewish tradition wrote blessings for many of them, ready and waiting. Today: blessings for wonders.
screen: `THE SKY GOES WHITE.` → `THE WHOLE SEA AT ONCE.` → `EVERYONE PULLS OUT THEIR PHONES.`

segments.voice: The Mishnah, the rabbis' first great law book, lists them. Each starts with the six words, and then gets its own ending. For lightning, and many say for shooting stars and high mountains: oseh ma'aseh vereishit, who makes the work of creation. As if the world is still being made, right now, in front of you. For thunder, and for great storms and earthquakes: shekocho u'gevurato malei olam, whose strength and might fill the world. For the great sea, when you haven't seen it in a while: who made the great sea. For a rainbow, a blessing that remembers the promise after the flood: who remembers the covenant, is faithful to it, and keeps his word. The story in Genesis says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "I have set My bow in the cloud." Some even teach not to stare at a rainbow too long, out of respect. And once a year, in the spring month of Nisan, when you first see fruit trees in blossom, there's a blessing for God, who left nothing lacking in the world, and created good creatures and good trees for people to enjoy. People go out looking for a blossoming tree just to say it. What these blessings share is something a psalm says well: "How manifold are Thy works, O LORD! In wisdom hast Thou made them all." And a quiet teaching hides inside the list. You can't plan most of these. You don't schedule lightning. The blessing is already there, waiting for the moment the world surprises you. All you have to do is notice, and answer.
screen: `LIGHTNING: THE WORK OF CREATION.` · `THUNDER: STRENGTH FILLS THE WORLD.` · `THE RAINBOW: A PROMISE KEPT.` · `TREES IN BLOSSOM, ONCE A YEAR.` · then, large: `HOW MANIFOLD ARE THY WORKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for one wonder to bless. Start right where you are. Settle, and breathe. Look out a window if there is one, or close your eyes and listen. The sky, a cloud, a tree, a bird, the light on a wall, rain. Let yourself be surprised by something ordinary for a moment, as if you'd never seen it. If you pray, you can offer one of the old endings: who makes the work of creation. If you don't, simply say wow, and mean it. The bell holds the time.
Blessings for wonders. For lightning, thunder, the sea, the rainbow and blossoming trees, blessings already waiting for the moment the world surprises you.
Your line: the world has blessings built in. Today, when something stops you, a sky, a tree, a storm, stop all the way and answer it. Day one hundred seventeen.

118.title: Blessing on seeing people
118.hook: blessings exist for seeing a great scholar, a ruler, or a friend not seen in a year
118.howItsDone: Jews say special blessings on seeing an outstanding Torah scholar, a great scholar of any people, or a head of state, and on seeing a close friend after thirty days (Shehecheyanu) or after twelve months (mechayeh hametim).

segments.voice: Yesterday, blessings for wonders: lightning, thunder, the sea, the rainbow, trees in blossom. Your line was the world has blessings built in. Today, the wonders walk on two legs. Day one hundred eighteen.

Picture the arrivals hall at an airport. The doors slide open, and someone comes through, pulling a suitcase, looking around. Across the rope, someone else spots them and just lights up. They haven't seen each other in a year. Maybe longer. There's a shout, a run, a hug that nearly knocks the suitcase over. Nobody in that moment thinks of it as a religious experience. But the Talmud does. It has a blessing for exactly this, and its words are some of the strongest in the whole prayer book. Today: blessing on seeing people.
screen: `THE ARRIVALS HALL.` → `A YEAR SINCE THEY LAST MET.` → `THE TALMUD HAS A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: The Talmud lists blessings for seeing people, the way it lists blessings for seeing the sea. When you see a great Torah scholar, you bless God, who has shared of his wisdom with those who revere him. And when you see a great scholar who isn't Jewish, there's a blessing too: who has given of his wisdom to flesh and blood. Think about that. The rabbis built into daily life a blessing for learning wherever it shows up, in anyone. There are matching blessings on seeing a king or a ruler: who has shared of his glory, and who has given of his glory to flesh and blood. You bless not the person, but the source of what you see in them. Now the friend. If you see a close friend after thirty days, you say Shehecheyanu, the blessing for firsts, who kept us alive and brought us to this time. But if it's been more than twelve months, the Talmud says something bigger: blessed is the one who revives the dead. Mechayeh hametim. It's the same phrase from the daily prayer about God's power to give life back. The rabbis aren't saying the friend was dead. They're saying something about how absence feels, and how a reunion feels. After a year, you've half let go. Seeing them again is like being given someone back. And it's honest the other way too: to someone who missed you for a year, you're a small resurrection. So a hug in an airport can be a blessing, and a Shabbat dinner can be one, and so can walking into the room where an old friend is waiting.
screen: `A GREAT SCHOLAR: WISDOM SHARED.` · `ANY SCHOLAR: WISDOM GIVEN.` · `A RULER: GLORY GIVEN.` · `A FRIEND AFTER A YEAR.` · then, large: `WHO REVIVES THE DEAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: greet an old friend today. First, find them. Settle, and breathe. Let a face come to mind, someone you haven't seen or spoken to in a long time. Picture their face when they laugh. Remember one thing you love about them. Now picture seeing them again: the doorway, the hug, what you'd say first. If you pray, you can bless the one who gave you this person. Then decide how you'll reach out today, a call, a message, a visit. The bell holds the time.
Blessing on seeing people. For a scholar, a ruler, and a friend not seen in a year: blessed is the one who revives the dead.
Your line: seeing you is a blessing. Today, reach out to that old friend, and if you can, tell them what seeing them means. Day one hundred eighteen.

119.title: Hard news
119.hook: on hearing of a death, Jews bless "the true judge", a blessing inside grief
119.howItsDone: On hearing of a death, many Jews say Baruch Dayan HaEmet; close mourners say the full blessing when they tear their garment (keriah) at the funeral, and visitors to a shiva house traditionally wait for the mourner to speak first.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blessing on seeing people, and a friend after a year. Your line was seeing you is a blessing. It's the end of a week of blessings: for food, after food, for firsts, for wonders, for people. Today, a harder one. Day one hundred nineteen.

Most of us know the moment. The phone rings at an odd hour, or a message starts with I'm so sorry. Someone has died. The mind goes blank, or it races. People reach for words and find the wrong ones: everything happens for a reason, at least they're not suffering, I know how you feel. We're uncomfortable with silence, so we fill it. Jewish tradition has words for this moment too, just three of them, said on hearing of a death. And then, just as important, it has a way of not saying anything more. Today: Baruch Dayan HaEmet.
screen: `A CALL AT AN ODD HOUR.` → `THE WRONG WORDS.` → `THREE WORDS, THEN SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Baruch Dayan HaEmet means blessed is the true judge. The Mishnah says that on good news, you bless the one who is good and does good, and on bad news, you bless the true judge. And it adds something startling: a person is obligated to bless over the bad just as over the good. That doesn't mean pretending the bad is good. The blessing doesn't say this is fine. It doesn't explain anything. It just says, in the worst moment: God is still God, and I'm still speaking to God, even now, even through this. Many people say the short form, just those three words, when they hear news of a death. Close mourners say the full blessing, with God's name, at the funeral, when they tear a piece of their clothing, keriah, an ancient sign of grief. The Bible has a line people often think of here, from Job, who lost everything: "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." And then comes the other half: the silence. When the priest Aaron lost two sons, the Torah says: "And Aaron held his peace." When Job's friends came to comfort him, they sat with him on the ground for seven days, and nobody said a word, because they saw how great his pain was. Their trouble started when they began to explain. Jewish mourning customs still carry this. At a shiva house, where mourners sit for seven days, visitors traditionally wait for the mourner to speak first. You don't arrive with a speech. You arrive with your presence. Three words of blessing, and then no explanations at all.
screen: `BLESSED IS THE TRUE JUDGE.` · `BLESS OVER THE BAD AS THE GOOD.` · `KERIAH: A TORN GARMENT.` · `AARON HELD HIS PEACE.` · then, large: `THE LORD GAVE, AND THE LORD HATH TAKEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with grief without explaining it. Go gently here. Settle, and breathe. Let someone you've lost come to mind, or a loss of another kind, or someone else's grief you've witnessed. Don't try to make sense of it. Don't look for the reason. Just let it sit beside you, the way Job's friends sat beside him on the ground. If you pray, you can say the three words, Baruch Dayan HaEmet. If you don't, simply let the silence hold it. The bell holds the time.
Baruch Dayan HaEmet. Blessed is the true judge: three words said on hearing of a death, a blessing inside grief that explains nothing.
Your line: even here, a word. Today, if you meet someone who is grieving, say less. Be there, and let them speak first. Day one hundred nineteen.

fork.setup: you walk into a shiva house. the mourner is sitting low, looking at the floor. you've prepared something to say. what does tradition suggest?
options: say your words right away, to fill the silence.
sit, and wait for the mourner to speak first.
explain why this might be for the best.
fork.reveal: visitors traditionally wait for the mourner to speak first: presence before words, and no explanations.

original.note: Hebrew: blessed is the true judge. emet, truth, is spelled with the first, middle and last letters of the alphabet.

trapdoor: what you thought: a religious condolence phrase.
what it means: three words that keep speaking to God inside grief, and then make room for silence.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Berakhot 9:2 and 9:5 (bless over the bad as over the good); Moed Katan 28b: comforters may not speak until the mourner begins.

sources.ref: Mishnah Berakhot 9:2, 9:5 (the true judge; bless over the bad)
Babylonian Talmud, Moed Katan 28b (mourner speaks first)
